claim: Assembly of bacterial ring-shaped hexameric replicative helicases on single-stranded (ss) DNA requires specialized loading factors.
source: Assembly of bacterial ring-shaped hexameric replicative helicases on single-stranded (ss) DNA requires specialized loading factors.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about bacterial helicase assembly, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: Five copies of λP bind at DnaB subunit interfaces and reconfigure the helicase into an open spiral conformation that is intermediate to previously observed closed ring and closed spiral forms.
source: We show that five copies of λP bind at DnaB subunit interfaces and reconfigure the helicase into an open spiral conformation that is intermediate to previously observed closed ring and closed spiral forms
evidence: This claim is supported by the cryo-EM structure determination and native mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Reconfiguration of the helicase by λP produces openings large enough to admit ssDNA into the inner chamber.
source: reconfiguration also produces openings large enough to admit ssDNA into the inner chamber
evidence: This is inferred from structural measurements showing ~15 Å and ~20 Å openings in the CTD and NTD layers.

claim: The helicase is observed in a restrained inactive configuration that poises it to close on activating signal and transition to the translocation state.
source: The helicase is also observed in a restrained inactive configuration that poises it to close on activating signal, and transition to the translocation state.
evidence: This is based on structural observations showing distorted ATP-binding and DNA-binding sites in the BP complex.

claim: Chromosomal replicative helicases are hexameric protein ensembles that travel ahead of the advancing replisome, dissolving duplex DNA into templates for DNA synthesis.
source: Chromosomal replicative helicases are hexameric protein ensembles that travel ahead of the advancing replisome, dissolving duplex DNA into templates for DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of replicative helicases.

claim: Melting of the duplex arises from ATP dependent translocation of the helicase along single stranded (ss) DNA, paired with inclusion/exclusion of DNA strands from an internal chamber.
source: Melting of the duplex arises from ATP dependent translocation of the helicase along single stranded (ss) DNA, paired with inclusion/exclusion of DNA strands from an internal chamber.
evidence: This describes the established mechanism of helicase function.

claim: In bacteria, replicative helicases are closed protein rings.
source: In bacteria, replicative helicases are closed protein rings
evidence: This is established knowledge about bacterial helicase structure.

claim: Bacteria use specialized loading factors that mediate opening of the protein ring, guiding of ssDNA into the exposed chamber, and sealing of the helicase with ssDNA trapped inside.
source: To assemble such entities on DNA, bacteria use specialized loading factors that mediate opening of the protein ring, guiding of ssDNA into the exposed chamber, and, finally, sealing of the helicase with ssDNA trapped inside (Soultanas, 2012; Bell and Kaguni, 2013; O'Donnell et al., 2013; O'Shea and Berger, 2014; Chodavarapu and Kaguni, 2016; Hauk and Berger, 2016; Bleichert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The architecture and mechanism of translocation of ring-shaped replicative helicases have been extensively studied.
source: The architecture and mechanism of translocation of ring-shaped replicative helicases have been extensively studied (Yu et al., 1996; Sawaya et al., 1999; Singleton et al., 2000; Yang et al., 2002; Enemark and Joshua-Tor, 2006; Núñez-Ramírez et al., 2006; Bailey et al., 2007a; Bailey et al., 2007b; Wang et al., 2008; Kashav et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2009; Thomsen and Berger, 2009; Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012; Kaplan, 2013; Robinson and van Oijen, 2013; Strycharska et al., 2013; Lee et al., 2014; Bazin et al., 2015; Fernández-Millán et al., 2015; O'Donnell and Li, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: Less is known about opening, assembly on ssDNA, and closing of the helicase as catalyzed by helicase loaders.
source: Less is known, however, of opening, assembly on ssDNA, and closing of the helicase as catalyzed by helicase loaders (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations indicating limited prior knowledge.

claim: Assembly of the bacterial replicative helicase on chromosomal DNA takes place during the initiation phase of DNA replication.
source: Assembly of the bacterial replicative helicase on chromosomal DNA takes place during the initiation phase of DNA replication (LeBowitz et al., 1985; Learn et al., 1997; Stephens and McMacken, 1997; Fok, 2002; Riazuddin, 2003; Stepankiw et al., 2009; Ozaki et al., 2012; Bell and Kaguni, 2013; Chodavarapu and Kaguni, 2016)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Four molecular elements cooperate to begin the process of assembling the replisome: a replication origin DNA sequence, the replication initiator protein, the replicative helicase, and the helicase loader.
source: In these systems, four molecular elements cooperate to begin the process of assembling the replisome. These elements are: a) a DNA sequence of length in the hundreds of basepairs called a replication origin, b) the replication initiator protein (E. coli: DnaA (Mott and Berger, 2007; Wolański et al., 2014; Leonard and Grimwade, 2015) V. cholera: DnaA, RctB (Egan and Waldor, 2003; Val et al., 2014; Gerding et al., 2015; Fournes et al., 2018), plasmids: RepE, Pi, TrfA (Konieczny et al., 2014), phage λ: O (Weigel and Seitz, 2006)), c) the replicative helicase, and d) the helicase loader.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing replication initiation systems.

claim: Multiple copies of the initiator protein bind to distinct sites on origin DNA and associate into a large protein nucleic acid complex that melts an A-T rich segment termed the DNA unwinding element (DUE).
source: Multiple copies of the initiator protein bind to distinct sites on origin DNA and associate into a large protein nucleic acid complex that is believed to have DNA around protein. One important output of this complex is melting of an A-T rich segment termed the DNA unwinding element (DUE).
evidence: This is established knowledge about replication initiation.

claim: The initiator protein DnaA has been shown to bind to the melted DUE segment.
source: The initiator protein DnaA has been shown to bind to this melted segment (Speck and Messer, 2001; Duderstadt et al., 2011; Chodavarapu and Kaguni, 2016; Bleichert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Recruitment of the replicative helicase to initiator-produced ssDNA at the origin proceeds through an assembly pathway with at least four stages.
source: Recruitment of the replicative helicase to initiator-produced ssDNA at the origin proceeds through an assembly pathway with at least four stages (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a conceptual framework supported by prior studies and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Stage I comprises the isolated hexameric DnaB helicase, which is found in two closed planar ring conformations, termed dilated and constricted.
source: Stage I comprises the isolated hexameric DnaB helicase, which is found in two closed planar ring conformations, termed dilated and constricted (Bailey et al., 2007a; Strycharska et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior structural studies.

claim: The dilated and constricted forms of DnaB differ on the relative orientation of subunits and the diameter of the central chamber.
source: these differ on the relative orientation of subunits and the diameter of the central chamber.
evidence: This is based on prior structural characterization of DnaB conformations.

claim: In Stage II, the loader captures the helicase, leading to inhibition of its ATPase and ssDNA translocation activities.
source: In Stage II, the loader captures the helicase, leading to inhibition of its ATPase and ssDNA translocation activities (Wahle et al., 1989a; Wahle et al., 1989b; Mallory et al., 1990; Davey et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior biochemical studies.

claim: E. coli DnaC serves as the helicase loader and delivers the DnaB helicase to the bacterial origin.
source: E. coli DnaC serves as the helicase loader and delivers the DnaB helicase to the bacterial origin
evidence: This is established knowledge about the E. coli replication system.

claim: DnaC is unrelated in sequence to λP, the loader that operates at the λ phage origin.
source: it is unrelated in sequence to λP, the loader that operates at the λ phage origin (Mallory et al., 1990), and which is the focus of this work.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: In Stage III, the helicase•loader complex engages ssDNA and the initiator protein at the origin.
source: In Stage III, the helicase•loader complex engages ssDNA and the initiator protein at the origin.
evidence: This is part of the conceptual framework of the helicase assembly pathway.

claim: Transition to Stage IV involves expulsion of the loader from the origin complex, with concomitant activation of the helicase's enzymatic activities, and assumption of the closed spiral conformer that can translocate along ssDNA.
source: Transition to Stage IV involves expulsion of the loader from the origin complex, with concomitant activation of the helicase's enzymatic activities, and assumption of the closed spiral conformer that can translocate along ssDNA (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The structure of the BP complex was determined using cryo electron microscopy (EM) and tomography to a resolution of 4.1 Å.
source: The structure of the BP complex was determined using cryo electron microscopy (EM) and tomography to a resolution of 4.1 Å (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplements 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, Table 1, and Appendix).
evidence: This is directly supported by the experimental data and methods described in the manuscript.

claim: Six DnaB protomers were unambiguously positioned in the EM map.
source: Six DnaB protomers were unambiguously positioned in the EM map that we obtained.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: Only five of six nucleotide-binding sites on CTD domains were populated, and with ADP.
source: Although the EM sample contained ATP, the density maps showed that only five of six nucleotide-binding sites on CTD domains were populated, and with ADP (below and Figure 2—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: Five copies of the λP helicase loader were visible in the density maps.
source: Five copies of the λP helicase loader were also visible in the density maps.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure determination.

claim: Cross-linking mass spectrometry (CX-MS) and binding studies were used to unambiguously assign the N to C chain polarity for λP.
source: Cross-linking mass spectrometry (CX-MS), along with binding studies (Figure 3A and B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 2 and Appendix), was used to unambiguously assign the N to C chain polarity for λP and develop a tentative assignment of the amino acid sequence to the structure.
evidence: This is based on experimental CX-MS and binding data.

claim: The unanticipated B6P5 stoichiometry predicted by the density map was verified using native mass spectrometry (MS).
source: The unanticipated B6P5 stoichiometry predicted by the density map was verified using native mass spectrometry (MS) (Figure 3C, Table 3 and Appendix).
evidence: This is based on native MS measurements.

claim: Native MS measurements revealed a predominant species with a mass of 446.3 kDa corresponding to a B6P5 entity.
source: Our measurements revealed a predominant species with a mass of 446.3 kDa corresponding to a B6P5 entity
evidence: This is based on native MS data.

claim: Additional species with masses of 472.8 kDa (B6P6) and 419.7 kDa (B6P4) were observed at lower intensities in native MS.
source: additional species with masses of 472.8 kDa (B6P6) and 419.7 kDa (B6P4) were observed at lower intensities.
evidence: This is based on native MS data.

claim: Compositional heterogeneity was eliminated when ssDNA derived from the Oriλ phage replication origin was included.
source: However, compositional heterogeneity was eliminated when ssDNA derived from the Oriλ phage replication origin was included.
evidence: This is based on native MS experiments with ssDNA.

claim: Native MS of the BP•origin ssDNA complex revealed a single entity with a mass of 459.5 kDa corresponding to the B6P5 complex bound to origin-derived 43-mer ssDNA.
source: Native MS of the BP•origin ssDNA complex revealed a single entity with a mass of 459.5 kDa; this mass corresponds to the B6P5 complex bound to origin-derived 43-mer ssDNA (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Table 3 and Appendix).
evidence: This is based on native MS data with ssDNA.

claim: Although ATP was included in both the ssDNA and ssDNA-free samples, native MS measurements showed no evidence that either complex included nucleotide.
source: Surprisingly, although ATP was included in both the ssDNA and ssDNA-free samples, native MS measurements showed no evidence that either complex included nucleotide.
evidence: This is based on native MS data.

claim: The BP complex presents as a three-layered ensemble with approximate dimensions of 135 Å x 150 Å x 120 Å.
source: The BP complex presents as a three-layered ensemble with approximate dimensions of 135 Å x 150 Å x 120 Å (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on measurements from the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Two layers of the BP complex correspond to the six NTD and CTD components of the DnaB-helicase, and the third layer represents the λP helicase loader.
source: Two of these layers correspond to the six NTD and CTD components of the DnaB-helicase, and the third layer represents the λP helicase loader.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The NTD and CTD layers of the BP complex exhibit a right-handed open spiral configuration.
source: The NTD and CTD layers of the BP complex exhibit a right-handed open spiral configuration
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The right-handed open spiral configuration of the BP complex is distinct from all previously described structures of the DnaB-helicase.
source: which is distinct from all previously described structures of the DnaB-helicase (Bailey et al., 2007a; Wang et al., 2008; Lo et al., 2009; Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012; Arias-Palomo et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2013; Strycharska et al., 2013; Bazin et al., 2015)
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior structures cited in the literature.

claim: The configuration of DnaB in the BP complex is reminiscent of the configuration of DnaB in the 25 Å EM map of E. coli DnaB bound to the DnaC helicase loader.
source: but is reminiscent of the configuration of DnaB in the 25 Å EM map of E. coli DnaB bound to the DnaC helicase (BC) loader (Arias-Palomo et al., 2013)
evidence: This is based on comparison with a prior low-resolution structure.

claim: Presence of the λP loader, in combination with the breached interfaces in the NTD and CTD layers, re-sculpts the central chamber of DnaB into a deep canyon that runs for ~90–100 Å along the entire length of the BP complex.
source: Presence of the λP loader, in combination with the breached interfaces in the NTD and CTD layers, re-sculpts the central chamber of DnaB into a deep canyon that runs for ~90–100 Å along the entire length of the BP complex
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The canyon in the BP complex is essentially open to solvent.
source: this canyon is essentially open to solvent.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural features of the BP complex.

claim: The dimensions of the canyon suggest that up to ~30 bp of DNA could be accommodated within.
source: The dimensions of the canyon suggest that up to ~30 bp of DNA could be accommodated within
evidence: This is inferred from structural measurements.

claim: The estimate of ~30 bp DNA accommodation compares well with measurements on the analogous DnaB•DnaC complex.
source: this estimate compares well with measurements on the analogous DnaB•DnaC complex (Fang et al., 1999), an entity of similar size to the BP complex.
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior measurements cited in the literature.

claim: In the BP complex, five copies of the λP helicase loader bind to five consecutive DnaB subunit interfaces.
source: In the BP complex, five copies of the λP helicase loader bind to five consecutive DnaB subunit interfaces.
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Each λP protomer is comprised of a helical domain that binds in a deep gulley formed by an interface between two adjacent DnaB CTDs.
source: Each λP protomer is comprised of a helical domain that binds in a deep gulley formed by an interface between two adjacent DnaB CTDs (Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The five λP protomers are deployed in a right handed spiral arrangement and exhibit an average rise per subunit of ~3.1 Å and a pitch of ~10 Å.
source: The five λP protomers are deployed in a right handed spiral arrangement and exhibit an average rise per subunit of ~3.1 Å and a pitch of ~10 Å (Below, Materials and methods, Appendix and (Lu and Olson, 2003)).
evidence: This is based on helical parameter analysis of the structure.

claim: Each λP protomer sends out a lasso-like segment that runs along the edge of the CTD and positions a λP helix against a site formed by the CTD and the linker helix of an adjacent DnaB subunit.
source: Further, each λP protomer sends out a lasso-like segment that runs along the edge of the CTD and positions a λP helix against a site formed by the CTD and the linker helix (residues 183–194) of an adjacent DnaB subunit (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Disposition of two λP protomers (λP2 and λP4) enables contacts to a nearby NTD.
source: In addition, owing to intrinsic asymmetry in the DnaB-helicase hexamer (below), disposition of two λP protomers (λP2 and λP4) enables contacts to a nearby NTD (DnaB residues 77–78; λP2 to chain E and λP4 to chain C, Figure 4B)
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: There are two types of λP – DnaB interfaces that differ on contacts to the NTD.
source: this feature gives rise to two types of λP – DnaB interfaces (Appendix) that differ on contacts to the NTD.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: The BP complex is organized around five sub-structures that each contain a heterotrimer comprised of a single λP and two DnaB chains.
source: Our analysis implies that the BP complex is organized around five sub-structures that each contain a heterotrimer comprised of a single λP and two DnaB chains.
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: The two types of λP•(DnaB)2 interfaces each bury a substantial amount of accessible surface area (~2200 Å and ~2600 Å).
source: The two types of λP•(DnaB)2 interfaces described above each bury a substantial amount of accessible surface area (~2200 Å and ~2600 Å; these values are lower limits owing to our incomplete λP model, which accounts for ~50% of the λP sequence, Appendix).
evidence: This is based on surface area calculations from the structure.

claim: The extensive interface between λP and DnaB is consistent with the observed high affinity between DnaB and λP.
source: This feature is consistent with the observed high affinity between DnaB and λP (Mallory et al., 1990).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural data and prior biochemical observations.

claim: λP forms an extensive interface with two flanking DnaB subunits, which comprises a form of molecular handcuffing.
source: The finding that λP forms an extensive interface with two flanking DnaB subunits, which comprises a form of molecular handcuffing
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Inhibition of translocation activity could arise through prevention of essential conformational changes by individual CTDs due to molecular handcuffing by λP.
source: leads to the overall conclusion that inhibition of translocation activity could arise through prevention of essential conformational changes by individual CTDs.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement and known mechanisms of helicase function.

claim: In the BP structure, the CTD layer is found in an open right-handed spiral staircase configuration.
source: In the BP structure, the CTD layer is found in an open right-handed spiral staircase configuration (Figure 5A and B and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the cryo-EM structure.

claim: Isolated DnaB (Stage I) is found in two closed planar ring configurations where the NTD and CTD tiers populate either the dilated or constricted configuration.
source: Isolated DnaB (Stage I) is found in two closed planar ring configurations where the NTD and CTD tiers populate either the dilated ((Bailey et al., 2007a; Wang et al., 2008), PDB: 2R6A) or constricted configuration ((Strycharska et al., 2013), PDB: 4NMN).
evidence: This is based on prior structural studies cited in the literature.

claim: The ssDNA bound complex (Stage IV) displays a hybrid arrangement with a constricted CTD layer and a dilated NTD tier.
source: However, the ssDNA bound complex (Stage IV) displays a hybrid arrangement with a constricted CTD layer and a dilated NTD tier ((Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012), PDB: 4ESV).
evidence: This is based on a prior structural study cited in the literature.

claim: Structural comparisons of various orthologs of DnaB from E. coli to those from A. aeolicus and G. stearothermophilus are justified by a high degree of structural and sequence conservation.
source: Structural comparisons of various orthologs of DnaB from E. coli (Stage II/III) to those from A. aeolicus (Stage I (Strycharska et al., 2013)) and G. stearothermophilus (Stage IV (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012)) are justified by a high degree of structural and sequence conservation ((Leipe et al., 2000), Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Appendix).
evidence: This is based on sequence and structural conservation analysis.

claim: In comparison to the constricted closed planar ring form, the CTDs in the BP complex exhibit a right-handed pseudo-helical configuration characterized by an average helical rise per subunit value of ~4.1 Å, and a helical pitch of ~16 Å.
source: In comparison to the constricted closed planar ring form (PDB: 4NMN), the CTDs in the BP complex exhibit a right-handed pseudo-helical configuration characterized by an average helical rise per subunit value of ~4.1 Å, and a helical pitch of ~16 Å.
evidence: This is based on helical parameter analysis of the structure.

claim: The CTDs in the BP complex exhibit an average helical twist of ~56.4° along the pseudo-helical axis.
source: Furthermore, we find that the CTDs exhibit an average helical twist of ~56.4° along the pseudo-helical axis.
evidence: This is based on helical parameter analysis of the structure.

claim: The CTDs in the ssDNA bound form (Stage IV) exhibit an average helical rise per subunit of ~7.4 Å, a helical pitch of ~27 Å, and an average helical twist of ~60°.
source: By contrast, the CTDs in the ssDNA bound form (Stage IV) exhibit an average helical rise per subunit of ~7.4 Å, a helical pitch of ~27 Å, and an average helical twist of ~60°.
evidence: This is based on helical parameter analysis of the ssDNA complex structure.

claim: The CTDs in the BP complex are inclined by ~20° towards the helical axis and the internal chamber, in comparison to those in the dilated closed ring form.
source: Superpositions with a λP1•(CTD)2 substructure against all pairs of CTDs from the closed planar ring (constricted and dilated), and the closed spiral forms shows that the CTDs in the BP complex are inclined by ~20° towards the helical axis and the internal chamber, in comparison to those in the dilated closed ring form (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is based on structural superposition and analysis.

claim: The reconfiguration of CTDs in the BP complex brings them into an arrangement that is close, but not identical, to that required for ATP hydrolysis as inferred from the corresponding nucleotide-binding site in the ssDNA form.
source: The resulting reconfiguration of CTDs in the BP complex brings them into an arrangement that is close, but not identical, to that required for ATP hydrolysis as inferred from the corresponding nucleotide-binding site in the ssDNA form (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and inference about catalytic competence.

claim: Changes to the pitch, twist, and inclination of the CTDs during the transition from the closed planar ring form to the open right-handed spiral in the BP complex give rise to an inner chamber in the BP complex with a diameter of ~20–25 Å.
source: Changes to the pitch, twist, and inclination of the CTDs during the transition from the closed planar ring form to the open right-handed spiral in the BP complex give rise to an inner chamber in the BP complex with a diameter =~20–25 Å
evidence: This is based on structural measurements.

claim: The diameter of the inner chamber in the BP complex is comparable to the constricted closed spiral form (PDB = 4ESV, diameter =~20–25 Å).
source: this value is comparable to the constricted closed spiral form (PDB = 4ESV, diameter =~20–25 Å)
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural measurements.

claim: The diameter of the inner chamber in the BP complex is slightly larger than the constricted closed planar form (PDB = 4NMN, diameter =~15 Å).
source: and slightly larger than the constricted closed planar form (PDB = 4NMN, diameter =~15 Å)
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural measurements.

claim: The diameter of the inner chamber in the BP complex is much smaller than the dilated closed planar form (PDB = 2R6A, diameter =~50 Å).
source: but much smaller than dilated closed planar form (PDB = 2R6A, diameter =~50 Å).
evidence: This is based on comparison of structural measurements.

claim: The CTD tier in the BP complex adopts the constricted configuration.
source: Thus, the CTD tier in the BP complex adopts the constricted configuration.
evidence: This is inferred from the diameter measurements of the inner chamber.

claim: The λP helicase loader reconfigures the CTD layer in the BP complex into a conformation that differs substantially from previously described DnaB structures.
source: The λP helicase loader reconfigures the CTD layer in the BP complex into a conformation that differs substantially from previously described DnaB structures.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: Reconfiguration of the CTD layer arises from displacements of the CTDs along the pseudo-helical axis to form the open right-handed configuration; the average pitch of the resulting entity is ~40% shorter than the ensemble in the ssDNA bound complex.
source: Reconfiguration arises from three broad types of changes: (1) displacements of the CTDs along the pseudo-helical axis to form the open right-handed configuration; the average pitch of the resulting entity is ~40% shorter than the ensemble in the ssDNA bound complex
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison.

claim: Reconfiguration of the CTD layer involves changes to the helical twist of individual CTDs along the helical axis; the CTDs in the BP complex are underwound by ~3.6° with respect to those in the closed planar ring and closed spiral forms.
source: (2) changes to the helical twist of individual CTDs along the helical axis; the CTDs in the BP complex are underwound by ~3.6° with respect to those in the closed planar ring and closed spiral forms
evidence: This is based on helical parameter analysis.

claim: Reconfiguration of the CTD layer involves inclination of the CTDs toward the helical axis; this change yields nucleotide-binding sites with configurations that are nearly optimal for catalysis.
source: (3) inclination of the CTDs toward the helical axis; this change yields nucleotide-binding sites with configurations that are nearly optimal for catalysis (below).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and inference about catalytic competence.

claim: Changes to the CTD layer cause the rupture of one of the six CTD interfaces, between subunits A and B, and produce a ~ 15 Å gap between the two CTDs that span the breached interface.
source: Collectively, these changes cause the rupture of one of the six CTD interfaces, between subunits A and B, and produce a ~ 15 Å gap between the two CTDs that span the breached interface
evidence: This is based on structural measurements.

claim: The ~ 15 Å gap in the CTD layer is large enough to permit entry of ssDNA into the central chamber of the helicase.
source: this gap is large enough to permit entry of ssDNA into the central chamber of the helicase.
evidence: This is inferred from the size of the gap.

claim: Within the BP complex, ssDNA binding is altered with λP making most, if not all, of the contacts.
source: Prior studies have established that, within the BP complex, ssDNA binding is altered with λP making most, if not all, of the contacts (Learn et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the literature.

claim: ATPase, and concomitantly, the helicase activities of the DnaB-helicase are suppressed by λP.
source: In addition, ATPase, and concomitantly, the helicase activities of the DnaB-helicase are suppressed by λP (Mallory et al., 1990).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the literature.

claim: The λP-binding site is more than 10 Å from both the ATP and DNA-binding sites.
source: However, the λP-binding site is more than 10 Å from both the ATP and DNA-binding sites.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements.

claim: Suppression of DNA binding and ATP hydrolytic activities must arise indirectly, as a consequence of structural changes induced by λP.
source: Suppression of DNA binding and ATP hydrolytic activities must, therefore, arise indirectly, as a consequence of the structural changes described above.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural data showing λP is distant from active sites.

claim: Alterations in the helical pitch, twist, and inclination of the CTD pseudo-helix in the BP complex combine to critically distort positions of six DNA-binding loops and the disposition of the subunits that form the composite ATP-binding sites.
source: We find that alterations in the helical pitch, twist, and inclination of the CTD pseudo-helix in the BP complex combine to critically distort positions of six DNA-binding loops and the disposition of the subunits that form the composite ATP-binding sites.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison.

claim: In the ssDNA complex, side chains from the DNA-binding loops of each DnaB protomer contact two phosphate groups per subunit along the helical path of the CTDs.
source: By example, in the ssDNA complex, side chains from the DNA-binding loops (G.st: R381, E382, G384; E. coli: R403, E404, G406) of each DnaB protomer contact two phosphate groups per subunit along the helical path of the CTDs (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on a prior structural study cited in the literature.

claim: In the BP complex, distortions in the disposition of the CTDs significantly shifts the DNA-binding side chains by distances ranging from ~3 to ~ 18 Å.
source: However, in the BP complex, distortions in the disposition of the CTDs significantly shifts the corresponding side chains by distances ranging from ~3 to ~ 18 Å (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison and measurements.

claim: The DnaB-helicase specifies six recA style nucleotide-binding sites, each of which resides at a protomer interface.
source: The DnaB-helicase specifies six recA style nucleotide-binding sites, each of which resides at a protomer interface.
evidence: This is established knowledge about DnaB structure.

claim: Five of the six nucleotide-binding sites in the BP complex are occupied by ADP, while the sixth site, whose composite architecture involves subunits that span the breached CTD ring, lies unfilled.
source: Although our EM samples were prepared with a large excess of ATP, we observe that five of the six sites in the BP complex are occupied by ADP, while the sixth site, whose composite architecture involves subunits that span the breached CTD ring, lies unfilled (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the cryo-EM density maps.

claim: Alterations to the relative orientations of the CTDs in the BP complex have remodeled the five filled nucleotide-binding sites into a configuration that is likely not optimal for catalysis.
source: Moreover, alterations to the relative orientations of the CTDs in the BP complex have remodeled the five filled sites into a configuration that is likely not optimal for catalysis.
evidence: This is inferred from structural comparison with the catalytically competent ssDNA complex.

claim: In the ssDNA complex, the Walker A and Walker B motifs from one CTD partner with K418 and R420 from the adjacent CTD to assemble an ATP-binding site.
source: In the ssDNA complex, the Walker A and Walker B motifs from one CTD partner with K418 and R420 from the adjacent CTD to assemble an ATP-binding site (Appendix).
evidence: This is based on prior structural analysis of the ssDNA complex.

claim: In the BP complex, changes in the relative disposition of the CTDs shift the positions of the alpha carbons associated with K440 and R442 away from those seen in the translocating ssDNA complex.
source: In the BP complex, however, we observe changes in the relative disposition of the CTDs that shift the positions of the alpha carbons associated with K440 (homolog of B.st K418 (the ssDNA complex)) and R442 (homolog of B.st K420) away from those seen in the translocating ssDNA complex (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The λP helicase loader induces a conformation of the DnaB helicase that is neither optimal for DNA binding nor ATP hydrolysis.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that the λP helicase loader induces a conformation of the DnaB helicase that is neither optimal for DNA binding nor ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural distortions of DNA-binding and ATP-binding sites.

claim: Observation of a distorted ssDNA-binding site implies that the DnaB-helicase, while complexed to λP, may not bind ssDNA as in the Stage IV translocating complex.
source: Observation of a distorted ssDNA-binding site implies that the DnaB-helicase, while complexed to λP, may not bind ssDNA as in the Stage IV translocating complex.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations.

claim: The distorted ssDNA-binding site in the BP complex is consistent with suppression of a crosslink between DnaB and ssDNA derived from the Oriλ replication origin when the λP loader is present.
source: This result is consistent with suppression of a crosslink between DnaB and ssDNA derived from the Oriλ replication origin when the λP loader is present (Learn et al., 1997).
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior biochemical data cited in the literature.

claim: The λP-enforced misalignment of the composite ATP-binding sites may explain lack of ATPase activity in the BP complex.
source: The λP-enforced misalignment of the composite ATP-binding sites may also explain lack of ATPase activity in the BP complex.
evidence: This is inferred from structural observations and prior biochemical data.

claim: The λP helicase loader makes few contacts to the NTD tier of DnaB in the BP complex.
source: The λP helicase loader makes few contacts to the NTD tier of DnaB in the BP complex
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The NTD tier of DnaB is reconfigured in the BP complex.
source: nevertheless, this tier is also reconfigured (Figure 7 and Videos 2 and 3).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The likely driver of NTD tier rearrangement is the λP-enforced remodeling of the CTD tier, which provides a reconfigured surface against which the NTD layer must pack.
source: The likely driver of rearrangement is the λP-enforced remodeling of the CTD tier, which provides a reconfigured surface against which the NTD layer must pack
evidence: This is inferred from the structural relationship between the CTD and NTD layers.

claim: Contacts by the λP2 and λP4 protomers to the NTD tier may contribute to NTD rearrangement, but to a small extent.
source: contacts by the λP2 and λP4 protomers to the NTD tier may also contribute, but to a small extent (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis.

claim: In comparison to the Stage I closed planar ring, the NTD layer in the BP complex exhibits an open spiral arrangement.
source: In comparison to the Stage I closed planar ring, the NTD layer in the BP complex exhibits an open spiral arrangement.
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The six N-terminal domains of the NTD layer feature a trimer of dimers configuration that displays pseudo-three-fold symmetry.
source: As with every other DnaB structure, the six N-terminal domains of the NTD layer feature a trimer of dimers configuration that displays pseudo-three-fold symmetry.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and comparison with other DnaB structures.

claim: The dimers that comprise the NTD layer in the BP complex are closely related to those in other DnaB structures (RMSD: 1.3 Å).
source: The dimers that comprise the NTD layer in the BP complex are closely related to those in other DnaB structures (RMSD: 1.3 Å, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D,E and Appendix).
evidence: This is based on structural superposition and RMSD calculations.

claim: The arrangement of dimers in the complete NTD layer exhibits a conformation that is distinct from that of other DnaB structures.
source: However, the arrangement of dimers in the complete NTD layer exhibits a conformation that is distinct from that of other DnaB structures (Figure 7)
evidence: This is based on structural comparison.

claim: The NTD layer arrangement in the BP complex is reminiscent to that seen in the DnaB segment of the low-resolution EM map of the E. coli DnaB•DnaC helicase loader complex.
source: though it is reminiscent to that seen in the DnaB segment of the low-resolution EM map of the E. coli DnaB•DnaC helicase loader complex (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B and Appendix).
evidence: This is based on comparison with a prior low-resolution structure.

claim: The NTD layer from the BP complex features a central chamber in the constricted state.
source: The NTD layer from the BP complex features a central chamber in the constricted state, surrounded by component domains in an open spiral configuration.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: The diameter of the BP NTD layer (~20–25 Å) is similar to that seen in the closed constricted planar form.
source: The diameter of the BP NTD layer (~20–25 Å) is similar to that seen in the closed constricted planar form
evidence: This is based on structural measurements and comparison.

claim: The diameter of the BP NTD layer differs markedly from the ~50 Å diameter of the corresponding structure in the ssDNA complex, which adopts the dilated conformation.
source: and differs markedly from the ~50 Å diameter of the corresponding structure in the ssDNA complex, which adopts the dilated conformation.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements and comparison.

claim: The NTD tier from the BP complex exhibits an average helical rise per subunit of ~2.6 Å, a helical pitch of ~7 Å, and helical twist values per subunit that ranged from ~40° to ~70° along the pseudo-helical axis.
source: Comparison of the helical parameters of the NTD tier from the BP complex (Materials and methods) to those of the constricted closed ring form revealed an average helical rise per subunit of ~2.6 Å, a helical pitch of ~7 Å, and helical twist values per subunit that ranged from ~40° to ~70° along the pseudo-helical axis.
evidence: This is based on helical parameter analysis.

claim: The ssDNA complex shows similar pseudo-helical parameters for the NTD layer: helical rise per subunit value of ~2.6 Å, a helical pitch of ~7.6 Å, and helical twist values per subunit that ranged from ~45 to 71°.
source: Nevertheless, we find that the ssDNA complex shows similar pseudo-helical parameters: helical rise per subunit value of ~2.6 Å, a helical pitch of ~7.6 Å, and helical twist values per subunit that ranged from ~45 to 71° (comparison of PDB entries: 4ESV and 2R6A).
evidence: This is based on helical parameter analysis of the ssDNA complex structure.

claim: Reconfiguration of the NTD layer in the BP complex into an open spiral creates a ~ 20 Å gap between the disrupted subunit interface.
source: Reconfiguration of the NTD layer in the BP complex into an open spiral creates a ~ 20 Å gap between the disrupted subunit interface.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements.

claim: The breach in the NTD layer is sufficiently large to provide access to the central chamber of DnaB to ssDNA.
source: As with the opening in the CTD layer, the breach in the NTD layer is sufficiently large to provide access to the central chamber of DnaB to ssDNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the size of the gap.

claim: Direct remodeling of the CTD tier by the λP helicase allosterically remodels the NTD tier.
source: Direct remodeling of the CTD tier by the λP helicase not only allosterically remodels the NTD tier
evidence: This is inferred from the structural relationship between the CTD and NTD layers.

claim: Remodeling by λP changes the relationship between the NTD and CTD tiers in the complete DnaB helicase.
source: but also changes the relationship between the NTD and CTD tiers in the complete DnaB helicase.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: In the closed planar structure, the NTD and CTD layers are essentially parallel.
source: In the closed planar structure, these two layers are essentially parallel.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the closed planar form.

claim: The CTD and NTD layers of DnaB in the BP complex make an angle of ~15°.
source: By contrast, the CTD and NTD layers of DnaB in the BP complex make an angle of ~15°
evidence: This is based on structural measurements.

claim: The corresponding angle between CTD and NTD layers in the Stage IV form is ~7°.
source: the corresponding value for the Stage IV form is ~7°.
evidence: This is based on structural measurements of the ssDNA complex.

claim: The NTD and CTD layers of the closed planar ring bury an extensive surface area (~7100 Å2).
source: The NTD and CTD layers of the closed planar ring bury an extensive surface area (~7100 Å2).
evidence: This is based on surface area calculations.

claim: The surface area buried between NTD and CTD layers in the BP complex is ~3100 Å2.
source: By contrast, the corresponding value for the BP complex is ~3100 Å2
evidence: This is based on surface area calculations.

claim: The NTD and CTD layers are held considerably less tightly in the loader complex than in the closed ring.
source: this implies that the NTD and CTD layers are held considerably less tightly in the loader complex than in the closed ring.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced buried surface area.

claim: Even in the absence of an extensive interface with the NTD layer, the λP helicase loader influences its organization.
source: We find that even in the absence of an extensive interface with the NTD layer, the λP helicase loader influences its organization.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural changes observed in the NTD layer.

claim: Reconfiguration of the CTD layer by λP programs the open spiral configuration of the NTD layer.
source: Reconfiguration of the CTD layer by λP programs the open spiral configuration of the NTD layer
evidence: This is inferred from the structural relationship between the layers.

claim: Alteration in the diameter of the central chamber is one change that accompanies transition of DnaB from the loader bound complex to that in the translocation state.
source: We also observe that alteration in the diameter of the central chamber is one change that accompanies transition of DnaB from the loader bound complex to that in the translocation state (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on comparison of structures from different stages.

claim: Opening the DnaB-helicase requires five λP helicase loaders, which bind to consecutive interfaces.
source: We observe that opening the DnaB-helicase requires five λP helicase loaders, which bind to consecutive interfaces
evidence: This is based on the cryo-EM structure showing five λP molecules bound.

claim: The ruptured sixth interface in the BP complex is not able to bind a sixth loader.
source: the ruptured sixth interface is not able to bind a sixth loader.
evidence: This is inferred from the structure showing only five λP molecules.

claim: The closed ring form of DnaB harbors two types of NTD interfaces, one of which (tail-to-tail) will likely require more energy to open than the second (head-to-tail).
source: The peculiar arrangement of isomers of DnaB protomers in the closed ring form suggests that the closed ring form of DnaB harbors two types of NTD interfaces (the CTD interfaces are equivalent), one of which (tail-to-tail) will likely require more energy to open than the second (head-to-tail) ((Wang et al., 2008; Strycharska et al., 2013), Figure 7, and Appendix).
evidence: This is inferred from structural analysis and prior studies.

claim: The interface that is breached in the BP complex is the weaker head-to-tail interface.
source: Indeed, the interface that is breached in the BP complex is the weaker head-to-tail interface.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis.

claim: Binding of individual loaders to DnaB could take place stochastically, with each binding event remodeling an interface until five have bound.
source: Thus, we speculate that binding of individual loaders to DnaB could take place stochastically, with each binding event remodeling an interface until five have bound.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Activation of the DnaB-helicase for translocation on ssDNA requires eviction of the ring-breaking helicase loader and concomitant sealing of the breaches in the NTD and CTD layers.
source: Activation of the DnaB-helicase for translocation on ssDNA requires eviction of the ring-breaking helicase loader and concomitant sealing of the breaches in the NTD and CTD layers (Figure 8—figure supplement 2 and Video 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural differences between the BP complex and the active helicase.

claim: The bacterial DnaK/DnaJ/GrpE chaperone apparatus engages at the lambda origin to partially dissolve the λP helicase loader from the BP complex.
source: An extensive body of insightful work has documented engagement of the bacterial DnaK/DnaJ/GrpE chaperone apparatus at the lambda origin to partially dissolve the λP helicase loader from the BP complex (LeBowitz et al., 1985; Mensa-Wilmot et al., 1989; Wyman et al., 1993; Polissi et al., 1995).
evidence: This is based on prior biochemical studies cited in the literature.

claim: Eviction of the loader from DnaB allows the helical CTD tier to relax into the configuration of the ssDNA complex by deploying to its full helical pitch (~27 Å).
source: In the first instance, eviction of the loader from DnaB allows the helical CTD tier to relax into the configuration of the ssDNA complex by deploying to its full helical pitch (~27 Å).
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of structures.

claim: Departure of the loader permits the CTDs to adopt a relaxed ~60° helical twist relationship around the pseudo-helical axis.
source: Second, departure of the loader permits the CTDs to adopt a relaxed ~60° helical twist relationship around the pseudo-helical axis.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of structures.

claim: The DNA binding and the ATPase sites, freed of constraints enforced by λP, assume productive conformations.
source: Third, the DNA binding and the ATPase sites, freed of constraints enforced by λP, assume productive conformations.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural distortions observed in the BP complex.

claim: Origin-derived ssDNA enters the inner chamber with expulsion of the loader.
source: Origin-derived ssDNA enters the inner chamber with expulsion of the loader.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanism for helicase activation.

claim: ssDNA in the inner chamber could drive closure of the CTD layer forward in the assembly pathway to the spiral form of the ssDNA complex, rather than backwards to the planar form.
source: One might speculate that ssDNA in the inner chamber could drive closure of the CTD layer forward in the assembly pathway to the spiral form of the ssDNA complex, rather than backwards to the planar form.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: Expulsion of λP enables exchange of ADP in the BP complex for ATP, which must take place for DnaB to assume the translocation competent form.
source: We speculate that expulsion of λP enables exchange of ADP in the BP complex for ATP, which must take place for DnaB to assume the translocation competent form (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: The unfilled nucleotide site at the breached interface will bind ATP, and this will further promote closing of the CTD tier.
source: As well, the unfilled nucleotide site at the breached interface will bind ATP, and this will also further promote closing of the CTD tier.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors.

claim: The CTD tier, freed of restraining interactions imposed by the λP loader, can undergo conformational changes expected during translocation.
source: Lastly, the CTD tier, freed of restraining interactions imposed by the λP loader, can undergo conformational changes expected during translocation (Itsathitphaisarn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural constraints observed in the BP complex and prior knowledge of translocation mechanisms.
